extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians in discrete geometry / combinatorial optimization (readers of the Kepler conjecture proof)
extracted.subtask_description: Verifying that the plane graph G(D) associated to a decomposition star D satisfies the finite list of 'tameness' properties, constructing admissible weight assignments, and eliminating graphs by linear-program relaxations as part of the Kepler conjecture proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: No loops or multiple joins
rubrics_metrics.description: The plane graphs associated with a decomposition star do not have loops or multiple joins.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Edges of G(D) are defined by triangles whose sides vary between lengths 2 and 2t0; the triangle angles are strictly less than π, so the edges of the metric graph on the unit sphere have arc-length strictly less than π and endpoints are never antipodal. A loop on the combinatorial graph would correspond to a closed geodesic; a multiple join would correspond to antipodal points joined by multiple minimal geodesics. By the arc-length constraints these configurations do not occur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tameness (overall)
rubrics_metrics.description: A plane graph is called 'tame' (Definition 7.3) if it satisfies a certain restrictive set of enumerated properties; Theorem 9.20: if D is a contravening decomposition star then G(D) is tame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show a contravening graph is tame, verify each of the defining properties of tameness (Properties 1–8 etc.). The proof proceeds by verifying each property in turn (Sections 10–11).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 1: face length bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The length of each face is at least 3 and at most 8.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower bound: by construction each face has at least three edges. Upper bound: Lemma 9.1 gives at most 8 edges. Aggregates formed in Remarks 9.18 and 9.19 have between 5 and 8 edges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 2: characterization of 3-circuits
rubrics_metrics.description: Every 3-circuit is a face or the opposite of a face.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The simplifications of the plane graph (Remarks 9.18 and 9.19) do not create new 3-circuits; see Lemma 9.9 for the formal argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 3: allowed 4-circuits (classification)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every 4-circuit divides the plane graph into two aggregates; a 4-circuit must surround one of the specific aggregates listed in Property 3 of tameness (cases enumerated in Proposition 10.13).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there are no enclosed vertices the 4-cycle is either a single quadrilateral face or a pair of adjacent triangles. If there is one enclosed vertex, the possibilities are: the enclosed vertex connected to three or four vertices of the quadrilateral (these are listed), and other configurations are ruled out by Lemmas 9.10 and 10.10 (e.g. two opposite connections give forbidden type (0,2), two adjacent connections are ruled out by Lemma 10.10). Choose the interior to have area ≤ 2π so it contains at most one vertex.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 4: vertex degree bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree of every vertex is at least 2 and at most 6.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lower bound: each vertex lies on at least one polygon so degree ≥2. Upper bound: impossibility of degree ≥7 follows from Lemma 9.8 for type (p,q), and Lemma 9.14 handles the (p,q,r) case (interior angles cannot sum to 2π).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 5: exceptional-face vertex degree
rubrics_metrics.description: If a vertex is contained in an exceptional face, then the degree of the vertex is at most 5.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 10.11: an exceptional standard region with a vertex of degree six must be pentagonal (Lemma 10.9); arrangements that would allow degree six at multiple vertices are excluded by Lemma 10.10, so contravening graphs cannot have such vertices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 6: face-length potential sum bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Sum over faces of c(len(F)) is at least 8 (Σ_F c(len(F)) ≥ 8).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 10.6 proves c(len(F))·pt ≥ σ_F(D) for each face (including aggregates), so summing over faces gives Σ c(len(F))·pt ≥ Σ σ_F(D) = σ(D) ≥ 8·pt. Proof treats three cases: face single standard region, pentagon aggregate from Remark 9.18, and aggregate of six regions from Remark 9.19 using σLP bounds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Property 8: nonadjacency of (4,0)-vertices
rubrics_metrics.description: There are never two vertices of type (4,0) that are adjacent to each other.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 10.5 cites [Hal97a, 4.2] for the proof that such adjacency cannot occur in a contravening plane graph.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissible weight assignment: existence and total weight bound
rubrics_metrics.description: Every contravening plane graph has an admissible weight assignment of total weight less than tgt = 14.8 (Theorem 11.1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given a contravening decomposition star D define w(F) = τ_F(D)/pt. Then Σ_F w(F) = τ(D)/pt < tgt = 14.8. The main task is to prove that this w satisfies the four defining properties of admissibility (Lemmas 11.2–11.4 and Proposition 11.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility property: face weight lower bound
rubrics_metrics.description: For a face F of length n, w(F) ≥ d(n).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 11.2: follows from Proposition 10.7 (τ_F(D) ≥ d(len(F))·pt), so the face weight meets the required lower bound function d(n).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility property: vertex-sum lower bound
rubrics_metrics.description: For a vertex v of type (p,q), the sum of weights of faces incident to v satisfies Σ_{v∈F} w(F) ≥ b(p,q).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 11.3: this property is established via Lemma 9.6, which gives lower bounds on the τ-sum at a vertex depending on its type (p,q).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility property: small (5,0)-vertex sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Let V be any set of vertices of type (5,0) of cardinality k ≤ 4; then Σ_{F: V∩F=∅} w(F) ≥ 0.55·k.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 11.4: uses Lemma 9.7 constants to guarantee a positive contribution (0.55·pt per such vertex) to τ-sum coming from tetrahedra not touching the faces that meet V.

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility property: separated-set inequality
rubrics_metrics.description: For any separated set V of vertices, Σ_{F: V∩F=∅} (w(F) − d(len(F))) ≥ Σ_{v∈V} a(tri(v)), where tri(v) is the number of triangles at v (tri(v) ∈ {0,..,4}).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposition 11.5 (proved through Lemmas 11.6–11.14): reduce to tri(v) ∈ {3,4} by showing tri(v)>2 in contravening graphs, treat cases using τLP and σLP bounds, handle aggregates (Remarks 9.18 and 9.19) separately, and partition V by equivalence classes of exceptional faces to sum inequalities. Constants a(p), d(n), b(p,q) and various LP-derived lower bounds are used throughout.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separated sets: structural constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Separated sets are vertex sets satisfying nonadjacency and other separation properties (see Section 7.2); they are used in the admissibility fourth property and must obey combinatorial restrictions (e.g. at most certain cardinalities on aggregates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Arguments in Section 11 use the separating properties to ensure triangles and quadrilaterals involved in inequalities are associated with well-defined exceptional-face equivalence classes; nonadjacency conditions limit how many separated vertices can lie on aggregates or hulls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of computer-verified inequalities (archive requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Many specific inequalities used in the proof are established by computer and recorded in an archive [Hal05]; each carries a nine-digit identifying number (e.g., calc-123456789).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To invoke a computer-proved inequality in the text, the inequality is stated precisely together with its identifying number (e.g., calc-927432550). The archive and its justifications are part of the formal evidence; interval arithmetic proofs are used to verify satisfaction of nonlinear constraints under interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Linear relaxation method for τ and σ bounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce linear variables for each τ_R and each interior angle α_R; substitute these linear variables into the nonlinear inequalities to obtain linear inequalities, and solve LPs to obtain bounds τLP(p,q,d) (lower bounds for τ-sums) and σLP(p,q,d) (upper bounds for σ-sums).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Given p triangles and q quadrilaterals at a vertex and an angle-sum constraint d, form an LP minimizing the sum of τ-variables subject to angle-sum constraints; LP solutions give guaranteed bounds for the nonlinear functions. This linearization/relaxation technique is repeatedly used to bound contributions at vertices and faces.

rubrics_metrics.name: LP relaxation interpretation conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: An interpretation I of an LP is a relaxation of the nonlinear program (NLP) if: (1) P = |I|, (2) the LP constraints are satisfied under the interpretation, and (3) f(p) ≤ c · x^I(p) for all p ∈ |I|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lemma 12.2: if these hold then the LP has a feasible solution and any upper bound M on the LP objective is an upper bound on the nonlinear function f over P. In practice satisfaction of constraints under the interpretation is verified by interval arithmetic or by LP-derived inequalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: LP-derived inequality technique
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a nonlinear inequality e·x ≤ b' is satisfied under an interpretation I, solve the LP max(e·x : A x ≤ b). If the LP maximum is ≤ b' then e·x ≤ b' holds under the interpretation (call this an LP-derived inequality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This provides a practical method to validate additional constraints under an interpretation once a base LP system A x ≤ b is known to hold under I.

rubrics_metrics.name: LP-sequence elimination criterion for tame graphs
rubrics_metrics.description: For a tame graph G (other than Gfcc, Ghcp, Gpent), construct a finite sequence of LPs such that (1) every LP has an admissible solution and optimal value < 8·pt, (2) each LP has an interpretation I that is a relaxation of σ maximization on a subset |I| ⊂ DS(G), and (3) the union of the |I| over the sequence equals DS(G).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Theorem 12.5: if such a sequence exists, then G cannot be contravening because every possible decomposition star for G is covered by some interpretation whose LP bound is < 8·pt. The construction is algorithmic and realized by computer; about 10^5 LPs are estimated overall for the classification.
